keep_reasoning: This highlights the knowledge gap and technical challenge that motivates the current study.

fact: Zebrafish are a useful model organism for studying Purkinje neuron intracellular dynamics in vivo during simple motor behaviors because they allow whole-cell patch clamp recordings in awake animals.
source_span: Zebrafish are a convenient model system for studying the intracellular dynamics of Purkinje neurons using whole-cell patch clamp recording in vivo in the context of simple motor behaviors.
keep_reasoning: This explains why the researchers chose zebrafish, which is important for understanding the experimental approach.

fact: The zebrafish cerebellum has three major parts, with the corpus cerebelli (CCe) and valvula cerebelli (Va) showing a three-layered architecture similar to mammals, and the study focused on Purkinje neurons in the CCe.
source_span: The zebrafish cerebellum has three major parts namely, the corpus cerebelli (CCe), the valvula cerebelli (Va) and the vestibulo lateral lobe which is subdivided into eminentia granularis and lobus caudalis cerebelli (Bae et al., 2009; Hibi and Shimizu, 2012). Of these only the CCe and Va show the characteristic three layered architecture (Hashimoto and Hibi, 2012). We have focused on Purkinje neurons in the CCe.
keep_reasoning: This provides anatomical background necessary to understand the experimental system and relevance to mammalian cerebellum.

fact: Zebrafish Purkinje neurons receive excitatory inputs from parallel fibers and climbing fibers and inhibitory inputs from stellate cells, similar to mammalian Purkinje neurons.
source_span: As in mammals, Purkinje neurons in zebrafish also receive excitatory inputs from parallel fibers (PFs) and climbing fibers (CFs) and inhibition from stellate cells (Figure 1A).
keep_reasoning: This fact explains the conserved circuitry underlying Purkinje neuron function, important for interpreting the findings.

fact: Unlike mammals, zebrafish Purkinje neurons do not project to deeper cerebellar layers but instead connect to eurydendroid cells, which are equivalent to mammalian deep cerebellar nuclear cells.
source_span: However, unlike mammals, zebrafish Purkinje neurons do not project to deeper layers but to efferent cells whose somata are present in the Purkinje cell layer or slightly ventral to it (Bae et al., 2009; Takeuchi et al., 2015). These efferent cells, also called the eurydendroid cells, receive short axons from the Purkinje neurons, send long projections outside the cerebellum (Bae et al., 2009; Heap et al., 2013; Takeuchi et al., 2015) and are equivalent to the mammalian deep cerebellar nuclear cells (Figure 1A).
keep_reasoning: This clarifies a key anatomical difference and functional analogy between zebrafish and mammalian cerebellar output pathways.

fact: Zebrafish Purkinje neurons express Zebrin II (aldolase-c, aldoca) in all cells, unlike mammals where it is expressed only in a subset of Purkinje neurons.
source_span: Zebrin II (aldolase-c, fructose bis-phosphate, a; aldoca) is expressed in all Purkinje neurons in zebrafish (Miyamura and Nakayasu, 2001; Bae et al., 2009), although it is expressed in only a subset of Purkinje neurons in mammals (Doré et al., 1990; Brochu et al., 1990; Leclerc et al., 1992; Sillitoe et al., 2004) and birds (Pakan et al., 2007; Iwaniuk et al., 2009; Corfield et al., 2015; Vibulyaseck et al., 2015).
keep_reasoning: This molecular marker fact is important for understanding how Purkinje neurons were identified and targeted in zebrafish.

fact: The aldoca promoter was used to fluorescently label Purkinje neurons in zebrafish to enable targeted whole-cell patch clamp recordings.
source_span: We use the aldoca promoter to fluorescently label Purkinje neurons specifically so as to target them for whole-cell patch clamp recordings (Tanabe et al., 2010; Takeuchi et al., 2015).
keep_reasoning: This explains the experimental strategy for identifying and recording from Purkinje neurons.

fact: In zebrafish, cerebellar cells begin differentiating at 3 days post fertilization (dpf), and a simple layered cerebellar structure forms by 5 dpf.

source_span: Purkinje neurons appear at 2.8 dpf and their numbers stabilize at around 300 neurons by 5 dpf (Bae et al., 2009; Hamling et al., 2015). By this stage, PF and CF inputs to Purkinje neurons are already present (Bae et al., 2009; Takeuchi et al., 2015; Hamling et al., 2015).

fact: This study demonstrates for the first time that Purkinje neurons in awake, unanesthetized larval zebrafish exhibit membrane bistability in vivo.

source_span: Numerous proteins accomplish their biological function by structural transitions such as hinge motions , domain rotations , or side chain reorientations [2] .
keep_reasoning: This background fact explains why studying collective motions is relevant to protein function.

fact: It is often unclear how functionally relevant quantities relate to collective atomic motions in proteins, and FMA helps to clarify these relationships.
source_span: For many proteins it is far from obvious how functionally relevant quantities are related to such collective atomic motions . In such cases , the proposed technique is expected to elucidate relations between collective motions ( i . e . protein dynamics ) and protein function .
keep_reasoning: This motivates the need for the new method and its potential impact.

source_span: Alternatively , the MCM can be biased to compute free energy differences between different functional states ( using , e . g . , umbrella sampling ) .
keep_reasoning: This shows how the method can be used to understand energetic aspects of protein function.

source_span: The success of the technique rests on two prerequisites: ( i ) The collective motion must be representable by a linear combination of the chosen basis set . At the same time , the basis set should not be too large to avoid overfitting .

fact: FMA also requires that there is sufficient correlation, linear or non-linear, between the functional quantity and the collective motion to be detectable.

keep_reasoning: This clarifies when the method can successfully identify functionally relevant motions.

source_span: Optimization of the collective vector via the Pearson coefficient is closely related to the construction of a model for as a linear function of a set of given collective coordinates . When using MI as correlation measure , a non-linear model for can be constructed from a general set of functions ( such as splines ) .
keep_reasoning: This fact explains the difference between linear and non-linear modeling approaches within FMA.

fact: The basis set of collective coordinates in FMA can include motions along principal component analysis (PCA) vectors, normal modes, or other coordinate systems such as dihedral angle rotations.
source_span: The given collective coordinates used as basis set may correspond to motions along PCA vectors , normal modes , or to motions in any other useful coordinate system such as rotations of dihedral angles .
keep_reasoning: This fact helps understand the flexibility and inputs of the method.

source_span: If these given coordinates have an intuitive meaning ( such as the hinge-bending mode in T4L ) , the derived model can quantify the contributions of intuitive collective motions to the variance of , and hence , provide a functional interpretation of the collective dynamics .
keep_reasoning: This fact connects the method to understandable biological motions, aiding lay explanation.

fact: Tissue light scatter limits the visualization of the microvascular network deep inside living mammals.
source_span: Tissue light scatter limits the visualization of the microvascular network deep inside the living mammal.
keep_reasoning: This fact explains a fundamental challenge in imaging small blood vessels inside living animals, setting the stage for the study's motivation.

fact: The mammalian eye is transparent and provides a noninvasive view of the microvessels of the retina, which is part of the central nervous system.
source_span: The transparency of the mammalian eye provides a noninvasive view of the microvessels of the retina, a part of the central nervous system.
keep_reasoning: This background fact explains why the retina is a useful window for studying microvascular blood flow noninvasively.

fact: Imperfections in the optics of the eye blur microscopic retinal capillaries and single blood cells flowing within, limiting early evaluation of microvascular diseases.
source_span: Despite its clarity, imperfections in the optics of the eye blur microscopic retinal capillaries, and single blood cells flowing within. This limits early evaluation of microvascular diseases that originate in capillaries.
keep_reasoning: This fact highlights a key technical limitation that prevents early detection of retinal microvascular diseases.

fact: The researchers used 15 kHz adaptive optics imaging to noninvasively measure single-cell blood flow in the retina of C57BL/6J mice.
source_span: To break this barrier, we use 15 kHz adaptive optics imaging to noninvasively measure single-cell blood flow, in one of the most widely used research animals: the C57BL/6J mouse.
keep_reasoning: This fact describes the novel imaging approach and model organism used to overcome previous limitations.

fact: Measured blood flow in retinal vessels ranged over four orders of magnitude across vessel diameters from 3.2 to 45.8 micrometers without requiring surgery or contrast dye.
source_span: Measured flow ranged four orders of magnitude (0.0002–1.55 µL min–1) across the full spectrum of retinal vessel diameters (3.2–45.8 µm), without requiring surgery or contrast dye.
keep_reasoning: This fact emphasizes the sensitivity and noninvasive nature of the measurement across a wide range of vessel sizes.

fact: Retinal neurons have exceptionally high metabolic activity and require timely and adequate nutrition and waste removal.
source_span: Retinal neurons have exceptionally high metabolic activity and demand timely and adequate nutrition and waste removal (Pournaras et al., 2008).
keep_reasoning: This biological background explains why precise blood flow regulation in the retina is critical.

fact: The retinal circulation supplies the inner retina with a stratified network of vessels, while the choroidal circulation supplies the photoreceptors.
source_span: Serving this need, the retinal circulation supplies the bulk of the inner retina with a stratified network of vessels, while the choroidal circulation supplies the photoreceptors.
keep_reasoning: This fact provides anatomical context for how blood supply is organized in the retina.

fact: The inner retina is typically fed by a single central retinal artery and drained by the central retinal vein in the holangiotic retina.
source_span: Anatomically, the inner retina is typically fed by a single central retinal artery while return is mediated by the central retinal vein in the holangiotic retina (Michaelson, 1954).
keep_reasoning: This fact gives important anatomical detail relevant to retinal blood flow.

fact: Functional characterization of blood flow in small retinal vessels is difficult because imaging single blood cells without invasive dyes requires very high spatial and temporal resolution and contrast.
source_span: However, functional characterization of perfusion has been more difficult, especially in the smaller vessels where imaging single blood cells without using invasive foreign dyes requires exquisite spatiotemporal resolution and contrast.
keep_reasoning: This fact explains the technical challenge that the study aims to address.

fact: Understanding blood flow dynamics at the scale of single cells in retinal capillaries is critical because blood flow is tightly linked to neural activity and nutrient delivery.
source_span: Understanding perfusion kinetics at this scale is critical to understanding the entire connected network, especially since blood flow dynamics are tightly linked to physiologically relevant neural loads (neural-glial-vascular coupling).
keep_reasoning: This fact connects blood flow measurements to neural function and health.

fact: Studying blood flow at the single-cell scale is important to characterize health and disease conditions that affect nutrient delivery and waste removal in capillaries.
source_span: Moreover, studying blood flow at this scale is important to characterize conditions of health and disease which place important constraints on single file blood flow where nutrient delivery and waste product removal take place.
keep_reasoning: This fact explains the clinical and biological importance of measuring single-cell blood flow.

fact: In the retina and brain, stoppage of blood perfusion leads to neuron death, as seen in diseases like branch retinal vein occlusion, central retinal artery occlusion, and diabetic retinopathy.
source_span: In the retina, as in the brain, there is a known linkage between stoppage of blood perfusion and death of neurons. These are manifest not only by transient blockages as seen in branch retinal vein occlusion and central retinal artery occlusion, but also in more insidious diseases such as diabetic retinopathy (Pournaras et al., 2008).
keep_reasoning: This fact links blood flow disruptions to serious retinal diseases and neuron loss.

fact: Retinal vascular diseases are often detected too late in the clinic, after vision loss or severe structural changes are visible.
source_span: Unfortunately, the detection of retinal vascular disease in the clinic often comes too late, when either the patient reports vision loss or when structural changes to the vasculature become severe enough to be visualized by clinical ophthalmoscopes.
keep_reasoning: This fact highlights the clinical problem motivating early detection methods.

fact: Many retinal vascular diseases are believed to start in capillaries, which are difficult to study due to their microscopic size, making early detection challenging.
source_span: Making matters worse, many vascular diseases of the eye are believed to manifest first in capillaries, which generally evade detailed study due to their microscopic size, thus making early detection in the clinic difficult.
keep_reasoning: This fact explains why capillaries are a critical but challenging target for early disease detection.

fact: Retinal capillaries have lumen diameters ranging from 3 to 7 micrometers and exhibit single-file blood cell flow.
source_span: Retinal capillaries with single file flow are small, with lumen diameter ranging from 3 to 7 µm (Guevara-Torres et al., 2016).
keep_reasoning: This fact defines the physical scale and flow characteristics of retinal capillaries.

fact: Conventional imaging systems like scanning laser ophthalmoscopy and optical coherence tomography have limited resolution (10–13 micrometers) and do not correct for eye aberrations, making them insufficient to image retinal capillaries.
source_span: This poses a challenge for conventional imaging systems, such as scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (SLO) and optical coherence tomography (OCT), which do not correct for the aberrations of the eye, and have an optical resolution of 10–13 µm (Porter et al., 2006; Zhi et al., 2012).
keep_reasoning: This fact explains why existing clinical imaging methods cannot resolve the smallest retinal vessels.

fact: Imaging larger vessels is complicated by densely packed single blood cells and non-parabolic velocity profiles, making accurate flow measurement difficult without detailed knowledge of flow patterns.
source_span: Imaging techniques that can visualize the larger vessels (~10–200 µm) are still faced with the problem that single blood cells (~6–8 µm) are densely packed and exhibit non-parabolic velocity profiles, making an accurate assessment of mean velocity and flow difficult without empirical knowledge of the profile shape.
keep_reasoning: This fact describes challenges in measuring blood flow even in larger retinal vessels.

fact: Detecting subtle functional changes in blood flow becomes harder as vessel size approaches the size of red blood cells due to the particulate nature of blood flow.
source_span: Detecting subtle functional changes to flow becomes exceedingly difficult as the ratio of vessel lumen to RBC diameter decreases, because of the particulate nature of blood flow.
keep_reasoning: This fact explains why small vessel imaging is especially challenging for detecting early disease changes.

fact: No device has yet noninvasively studied single-cell blood flow dynamics across the full range of retinal vessel sizes in living mice or humans.
source_span: Due to the above challenges, a device that can noninvasively study single-cell blood flow dynamics in the full range of retinal vessel sizes in the living body has not yet been demonstrated, in either the mouse or human.
keep_reasoning: This fact states the technological gap the study aims to fill.

fact: Doppler-based imaging techniques can measure bulk blood velocity in large and medium-sized retinal vessels but are limited in small vessels due to fewer blood cells and optical resolution constraints.
source_span: Studies in larger retinal vessels using Doppler strategies have provided one solution to report bulk velocity... However, applying the Doppler approach to small vessels is challenging as there are far fewer blood cells at the capillary level, thereby reducing the Doppler signature. Additionally, left uncorrected, the smallest measurement beam that can be formed is limited by the imperfect optics of the eye (~10–13 µm spot size).
keep_reasoning: This fact explains the limitations of Doppler imaging for small vessel blood flow.

fact: Doppler imaging can be contaminated by signals from adjacent vessels or deeper retinal layers, complicating accurate measurement of single vessel blood flow.
source_span: Such techniques also suffer the consequence of contamination of adjacent vessel signal which may be of opposite direction or speed. Axial contributions from deeper vessels may also contaminate single vessel measurement as retinal vessels above and below the interrogation beam can introduce non-specific signals.
keep_reasoning: This fact describes a technical limitation affecting the accuracy of Doppler-based flow measurements.

fact: Doppler optical coherence tomography (OCT) improves some limitations but still only reliably measures blood flow in large retinal vessels in mice and large to medium vessels in humans.
source_span: Doppler OCT has mitigated this issue to some extent; however, signal-to-noise and lateral resolution still limit the signal readout of absolute velocity or flow to only the large retinal vessels in mice, and large and medium-sized vessels in humans.
keep_reasoning: This fact clarifies the current capabilities and limits of Doppler OCT.

fact: Optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) can visualize perfused versus non-perfused capillaries but does not quantify blood flow or velocity.
source_span: Towards achieving capillary resolution, OCT angiography (OCTA) has recently revolutionized measures of perfused vs. non-perfused capillaries. However, it does not quantitate blood flow or velocity.
keep_reasoning: This fact explains the strengths and limitations of OCTA in retinal blood flow assessment.

fact: OCTA cannot detect conditions of hyper- or hypo-perfusion, so early functional changes in blood flow may be missed and only later structural vessel occlusions are visualized.
source_span: Conditions of hyper- and hypo-perfusion are not reported and thus early and subtle functional changes in blood flow may be overlooked and only later structural vessel occlusions visualized in disease.
keep_reasoning: This fact highlights a clinical limitation of OCTA for early disease detection.

fact: Adaptive optics (AO) ophthalmoscopy corrects for high order aberrations of the eye and achieves approximately 1–2 micrometer lateral resolution in vivo.
source_span: This has been possible as AO measures and corrects for high order aberrations of the eye, achieving ~1–2 µm lateral resolution in vivo (Liang et al., 1997; Roorda and Duncan, 2015; Roorda et al., 2002).
keep_reasoning: This fact explains the technical advantage of AO imaging for resolving small retinal structures.

fact: Adaptive optics ophthalmoscopy has enabled measurement of single blood cell speed in retinal capillaries in humans and mice, as well as in medium-sized vessels in humans.
source_span: In recent years, adaptive optics (AO) ophthalmoscopy has enabled reporting of single blood cell speed in capillaries in humans... and mice... and medium-sized vessels in humans.
keep_reasoning: This fact shows the progress and applicability of AO imaging to study retinal blood flow at the single-cell level.

fact: Adaptive optics (AO) imaging corrects for distortions in the eye and achieves about 1–2 micrometer lateral resolution in living eyes.
source_span: This has been possible as AO measures and corrects for high order aberrations of the eye , achieving ~1–2 µm lateral resolution in vivo ( Liang et al . , 1997; Roorda and Duncan , 2015; Roorda et al . , 2002 ) .
keep_reasoning: This fact explains the imaging technology that enables detailed, noninvasive visualization of retinal blood flow, which is central to the study.

fact: Phase contrast imaging approaches allow visualization of translucent properties of blood cells and vessel walls without using invasive dyes or contrast agents.
source_span: Recent advances ( Chui et al . , 2012; Guevara-Torres et al . , 2015; Scoles et al . , 2014 ) in developing phase contrast approaches has enabled visualization of translucent cell properties , like blood cell rheology ( Guevara-Torres et al . , 2016 ) and blood vessel wall structure ( Burns et al . , 2014; Chui et al . , 2014; Chui et al . , 2012; Sulai et al . , 2014 ) , without the aid of invasive foreign dyes or particles .
keep_reasoning: This fact highlights a key noninvasive imaging advance that makes the study's measurements possible and clinically relevant.

fact: Using very fast camera speeds combined with adaptive optics phase contrast imaging, researchers can resolve single red blood cells flowing in capillaries without using external contrast agents.
source_span: Recently , we combined this approach with extremely fast camera speeds to resolve densely packed RBCs in single file flow in capillaries ( 3 . 2–6 . 5 µm size ) and reported single-blood-cell flux ( Guevara-Torres et al . , 2016 ) without using exogenous contrast agents .
keep_reasoning: This fact describes the technical innovation enabling direct measurement of single-cell blood flow, a core advance of the study.

fact: Measuring blood flow across the full range of vessel sizes in the mammalian retina has been difficult due to the large scale and high cell flow rates, requiring automation for quantitative analysis.
source_span: While the above studies employing adaptive optics have enabled noninvasive measurement of single-cell velocity , measurement of blood flow in the full range of vessel sizes of the mammalian retinal circulation is yet to be achieved . This has partly been a problem of scale as automation is needed to perform quantitative measurements in larger vessels containing hundreds of thousands of blood cells flowing per second .
keep_reasoning: This fact explains the main technical challenge the study addresses, motivating the development of automated analysis.

fact: The mouse retina is a widely used model for human retinal physiology and disease, but there are few studies measuring retinal blood flow in mice, partly because mouse retinal vessels are much smaller than human vessels.
source_span: The mouse is the most widely used laboratory animal , yet there is a paucity of studies providing measures of retinal blood flow in the same . This gap need be addressed as the mouse has been and continues to be used to model human retinal physiology , including blood flow . The challenge of imaging mouse retinal blood flow is attributed to the difficulties of imaging its rather small eye , with even the largest vessels being only a quarter the size of the largest human retinal vessel .
keep_reasoning: This fact provides important biological and translational context for why the study focuses on mouse retinal blood flow.

fact: Characterizing normal blood flow throughout the entire retinal vascular tree in healthy mice will support future research on retinal and systemic vascular diseases using mouse models.
source_span: Given the importance of the laboratory mouse , with its completely sequenced genome and many models of disease , characterization of normative blood flow in the complete vascular tree of the healthy C57BL/6J mouse will propagate future research in a vast number of mouse models of retinal disease and systemic vascular disease .
keep_reasoning: This fact explains the broader significance and potential impact of establishing baseline blood flow measurements in mice.

fact: The study uses custom imaging strategies and algorithms to noninvasively measure single blood cells flowing in mouse retinal vessels ranging from 3.2 to 45.8 micrometers in diameter without using contrast agents.
source_span: In this study , we innovate imaging strategies as well as deploy custom algorithms to image single blood cells noninvasively in the smallest to largest vessels of the mouse retinal circulation ( lumen diameters: 3 . 2–45 . 8 µm ) ; without requiring exogenous contrast agents to facilitate measurement .
keep_reasoning: This fact summarizes the methodological innovation enabling comprehensive measurement of blood flow across vessel sizes.

fact: Blood flow rates measured per vessel in the mouse retina vary over four orders of magnitude, from the largest vessels near the optic disk to the smallest capillaries.
source_span: Measured flow rate per vessel ranged four orders of magnitude ( 0 . 0002–1 . 55 µL min–1 ) across the complete retinal vascular tree , from the largest vessel near the optic disk to the smallest capillary .
keep_reasoning: This fact highlights the wide dynamic range of blood flow in the retinal circulation, important for understanding retinal physiology.

fact: The noninvasive imaging approach provides multiple indicators of microvascular blood flow, including cell velocity, vessel diameter, flow rate, single-cell flux in capillaries, pulsatile flow, and spatial and temporal flow variations.
source_span: In addition to aiding basic science investigation , the noninvasive approach provides a comprehensive array of bioreporters of microvascular perfusion , including: cell velocity , lumen diameter , flow rate , single-cell flux in capillaries , pulsatile and cross-sectional flow , and indices of intrinsic temporal and spatial modulations in flow .
keep_reasoning: This fact explains the breadth of physiological information accessible with the new imaging method.

fact: This study provides the first measurements of cross-sectional blood cell velocity profiles and absolute pulsatile blood cell velocity in the mouse retina.
source_span: To our knowledge , we provide the first measurement of cross-sectional blood-cell velocity profile and the first absolute measurement of pulsatile blood-cell velocity in the mouse retina .
keep_reasoning: This fact states a novel and important scientific contribution of the study.

fact: The study also provides the first measurements of mean and pulsatile velocity and flow rate in medium and small retinal vessels, including capillaries, in mice.
source_span: We also provide the first measures of mean ( and pulsatile ) velocity and flow rate in medium and small vessels ( capillaries ) of the mouse retina .
keep_reasoning: This fact highlights the study's novel contribution to understanding blood flow in smaller retinal vessels.

fact: There is a heterogeneous distribution of velocity, flux, and other hemodynamic parameters across retinal vessels of different sizes and generations, indicating that vessel diameter alone poorly predicts microcirculation dynamics in the central nervous system.
source_span: We found that there is a heterogenous distribution of velocity , flux and other hemodynamic parameters in vessels of varying generation/size , showing that diameter alone is a poor predictor of microcirculation hemodynamics in the central nervous system .
keep_reasoning: This fact reveals an important biological insight about retinal blood flow regulation.

fact: Imaging the complete and intact retinal perfusion system in living mammals provides a valuable way to study microvascular blood flow dynamics in deep brain-like tissues noninvasively.
source_span: Through the innovations presented in this work , imaging the complete and intact perfusion system of the mammalian retina bridges an important gap in studying perfusion dynamics in deep microvascular beds within the living body . Due to the central nervous system origin of the retina , this method provides a powerful way to noninvasively study microvascular integrity and kinetics in a portion of the living brain .
keep_reasoning: This fact connects the retinal imaging approach to broader neuroscience and clinical relevance.

fact: Single blood cells in mouse retinal vessels were directly imaged using the confocal mode of adaptive optics scanning light ophthalmoscopy (AOSLO) without contrast agents.
source_span: Single blood cells were directly imaged using the confocal mode of AOSLO ( Figure 1 ) . 2D raster video captured at 25 frames per second revealed movement of a dense array of tightly packed RBCs traveling in vessels without requiring contrast agents ( Video 1 ) .
keep_reasoning: This fact describes the imaging modality and its noninvasive capability, foundational for the study.

fact: 1D line-scans across retinal vessels produce space-time images where moving blood cells appear as streaks, allowing measurement of their velocity with high temporal resolution.
source_span: Sequentially capturing 1D line-scans across the same vessel produced a space-time image of moving blood cells with a line resolution of 15 kHz ( Figure 1D , Figure 2 ) . Single cells produce an increase in backscatter providing positive contrast streaks which represent the displacement over time of each cell .
keep_reasoning: This fact explains the imaging data format and how blood cell movement is quantified.

fact: The maximum measurable blood cell velocity using the line-scan technique is much higher than the fastest blood cell velocities observed in the retinal circulation, ensuring accurate velocity measurement.
source_span: Based on the shallowest angle of beam intersection , the maximum velocity that could be measured using this technique was 1275 mm s–1 , which far exceeds the possible velocities of blood cells in the retinal circulation .
keep_reasoning: This fact confirms the technical adequacy of the measurement method for retinal blood flow.

fact: The Radon transform algorithm can automatically measure the slope of blood cell streaks in space-time images, enabling automated velocity determination in densely packed blood flow data.
source_span: The Radon transform was able to measure the slope of blood cell streaks within a dense array of overlapping regions of interest ( ROIs ) in a space-time image ( Figure 3A ) . ROIs with dominant streak orientations ( Figure 3B ) produced strong peaks in the Radon sinugram ( Figure 3C ) . The angle corresponding to the maximum Radon standard deviation gave the velocity of the cells in the ROI ( Figure 3D , Equation . ( 1 ) .
keep_reasoning: This fact describes the key computational advance enabling automated, high-throughput blood velocity measurement.

fact: Blood cell velocity in retinal vessels can reach up to approximately 100 mm per second, representing the upper limit of blood flow speed in the largest vessels of the eye.
source_span: From our data , we observed velocities of up to ~100 mm s–1 which represents the upper limit of blood velocity in the eye corresponding to center-line flow of the largest vessels .
keep_reasoning: This fact provides a key quantitative context for understanding blood flow speeds in retinal vessels, important for interpreting the study's velocity measurements.

fact: Motion correction algorithms are necessary to accurately measure low blood cell velocities in retinal imaging by compensating for small eye movements.
source_span: The lowest velocity was bounded by the motion correction algorithm which adjusted for small eye motion artifacts . Without motion correction , the lowest velocity observed was 0 mm s–1 ( corresponding to stuck or stationary blood cells ) .
keep_reasoning: Explaining the need for motion correction helps lay readers understand challenges in measuring blood flow in the eye and why the method is reliable.

fact: Removing static features such as vessel walls and retinal tissue through background subtraction improves the detection of moving blood cells in retinal imaging.
source_span: Quality of data was often improved when static features such as the vessel wall and other retinal tissue were removed through a running background subtraction of 10 ms ( Figure 2 ) , which improved signal detection of blood cells .
keep_reasoning: This fact explains a key image processing step that enhances the clarity of blood flow measurements, aiding understanding of the method.

fact: The velocity measurement algorithm selectively reports blood cell velocities only inside the vessel lumen, rejecting signals from outside the vessel.
source_span: The algorithm performed favourably to report only the velocities inside the vessel lumen . While analysis was enabled on the entire image ( including portions inside and outside the vessel ) , only velocities inside the vessel met the SNR calculation ( Equation 3 ) .
keep_reasoning: This fact clarifies that the method accurately isolates blood flow within vessels, which is critical for valid measurements.

fact: A signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) threshold of approximately 2.5 was used to ensure that only strong, reliable velocity data were accepted, matching human expert performance.
source_span: The SNR threshold that matched human performance was at SNR ~ 2 . 5 , meaning a fairly strict criterion measured only the strongest data .
keep_reasoning: This fact explains how data quality was controlled, important for understanding the reliability of the velocity measurements.

fact: The custom MATLAB code developed for this study can analyze space-time images of retinal blood flow at a rate of about 23 regions of interest per second, enabling detailed velocity profiling.
source_span: Our custom MATLAB code completed automated analysis of a typical space-time image ( Figure 4 ) at a rate of ~23 . 4 ROIs per second ( on a 3 . 7 GHz Intel i7-4820K processor , 16 GB RAM , 64-bit Windows 7 ) .
keep_reasoning: This fact highlights the computational efficiency of the method, which supports detailed and timely analysis of blood flow.

fact: Pulsatile blood flow corresponding to the cardiac cycle was observed in all retinal arterioles and venules imaged, demonstrating rhythmic variations in blood velocity.
source_span: Pulsatile velocity was observed in all 33 arterioles and venules imaged .
keep_reasoning: This is a core finding showing that blood flow in retinal vessels varies with the heartbeat, important for understanding vascular dynamics.

fact: Pulsatile blood flow was also routinely observed in retinal capillaries, contrary to previous assumptions that capillary flow is steady.
source_span: Contrary to conventional thought , pulsatile flow was also routinely observed in capillaries ( Guevara-Torres et al . , 2016 ) .
keep_reasoning: This challenges existing beliefs and is a significant novel observation relevant to retinal microcirculation.

fact: The measured heart rates from retinal blood flow velocity matched well with external pulse oximeter readings, confirming the accuracy of the retinal measurements.
source_span: We confirmed measurements of heart rate with external paw-clip pulse oximetry ( PhysioSuite , Kent Scientific Corp . , Connecticut , USA ) in a subset of vessels . The retinal-vessel measurement of heart rate and an alternate recording performed with the paw-clip pulse oximeter showed strong correlation with correspondence slope of 0 . 99 ( Figure 5C , linear fit with forced zero intercept , R2 = 0 . 89 ) .
keep_reasoning: This fact validates the retinal blood flow measurement method by comparison to an established heart rate measurement technique.

fact: Eye motion artifacts were ruled out as a source of the pulsatile velocity signal because eye movement velocities were much smaller and did not match the frequency or phase of blood flow pulsations.
source_span: The velocity of the largest eye motion was at least 23 times smaller than the velocity of blood cells ( Figure 5A ) . Moreover , the frequency and phase eye motion did not match the pulsatile velocity modulations ( Figure 5B ) . Together , these findings rule out that the velocity signal is an artifact of either respiration or cardiac cycle related eye motion .
keep_reasoning: This fact addresses a potential confound and confirms that the pulsatile flow measurements reflect true blood flow, not eye movement.

fact: Arterioles and venules in the retina show different pulsatile blood flow waveforms, with arterioles having a steep leading edge and higher pulsatility index compared to venules.
source_span: Generally , arterioles had a steep leading edge of the velocity waveform whereas venules had a dampened waveform , due to vascular compliance and network hemodynamics upstream and downstream the imaged vessel . Using vascular indices described by Equations 4–6 above , we found that in an arteriole and venule of the same vessel generation , the arteriole had a much higher pulsatility index ( PI ) consistent with physiology of the cardiovascular system ( Figure 4—figure supplement 1 , PI = 0 . 67 for 25 . 3 µm arteriole vs PI = 0 . 18 for 33 . 5 µm venule ) .
keep_reasoning: This fact explains physiological differences in blood flow dynamics between vessel types, important for interpreting vascular function.

fact: Arterioles routinely showed a temporally asymmetric blood flow waveform indicating a bolus pressure wave followed by vascular relaxation, unlike venules which had more symmetric waveforms.
source_span: Furthermore , arterioles routinely showed a temporally asymmetric waveform indicating a bolus pressure wave followed by relaxation of vascular compliance ( Figure 4G , arteriole asymmetry index ( AI ) = 2 . 8 ) . This waveform is contrasted to what is seen in a venule in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 ( venular AI = 1 . 75 ) .
keep_reasoning: This fact provides insight into the mechanical properties and function of different vessel types in the retina.

fact: The average pulsatile blood flow waveform in retinal vessels is highly repeatable across cardiac cycles, demonstrating consistent vascular dynamics.
source_span: The average pulsatile waveform showed a high degree of repeatability . This is shown by way of example in the small error bars in Figure 4G which represents n = 35 cycles averaged in a single arteriole .
keep_reasoning: This fact supports the reliability and physiological relevance of the measured pulsatile flow patterns.

fact: The cardiac cycle modulates blood flow velocity across the entire vessel lumen in retinal arterioles, with an average heart rate of about 218 beats per minute in anesthetized mice.
source_span: The influence of cardiac pulsatility is seen across the vessel lumen , with an average periodicity of the cardiac cycles of 218 beats per minute ( bpm ) ( Figure 4F ) . Measured heart rate ranged from 186 to 302 bpm across all mice imaged , consistent with the reported range for the anesthetized mouse .
keep_reasoning: This fact links blood flow dynamics to heart function and provides physiological context for the animal model.

fact: Arterioles and venules in the mouse retina show different blood flow characteristics, including differences in pulsatility index and waveform shape.
source_span: Such functional difference between arterioles and venules can also be visually observed in Figure 9C , where vessels A1 and V1 have similar mean velocity , but markedly different PIs . Furthermore , arterioles routinely showed a temporally asymmetric waveform indicating a bolus pressure wave followed by relaxation of vascular compliance ( Figure 4G , arteriole asymmetry index ( AI ) = 2 . 8 ) . This waveform is contrasted to what is seen in a venule in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 ( venular AI = 1 . 75 ) .
keep_reasoning: This fact highlights key physiological differences between arterioles and venules that are important for understanding retinal blood flow dynamics.

fact: Red blood cell (RBC) velocity profiles in retinal vessels do not follow the classic parabolic flow model expected for Newtonian fluids.
source_span: Unlike models of Newtonian/laminar flow , the RBC velocity profile was poorly fit with a parabolic model that is bounded by zero velocity at the lumen surface ( Figure 6 ) .
keep_reasoning: This challenges common assumptions about blood flow and is important for accurately modeling retinal microcirculation.

fact: A small cell-free zone and the vascular glycocalyx prevent red blood cells from contacting the vessel wall in retinal microvessels.
source_span: A small cell-free zone combined with the vascular glycocalyx represented prevents cell contact with the vascular lumen at the microscopic scale .
keep_reasoning: This explains why RBC velocity near the vessel wall differs from classical flow models and is relevant for understanding microvascular blood flow.

fact: Assuming parabolic flow in retinal vessels can lead to a significant underestimation (about 39%) of mean blood flow rate.
source_span: An assumption of parabolic flow ( Vmax/Vmean = 2 ) leads to a 39% underestimation in mean flow rate in the vessel shown .
keep_reasoning: This fact is critical for interpreting blood flow measurements and improving accuracy in retinal hemodynamics.

fact: Local disruptions in capillary blood flow can be compensated by adjacent capillaries at low severity, but increased severity can lead to abnormal perfusion and structural changes in larger feeding and draining vessels.

As the severity and frequency of such local disruptions increase in disease, a tipping point may be reached when neighboring capillaries can no longer accommodate the extra workload they receive from decreased or no perfusion in affected capillaries. This can lead to a cascade of events where larger vessels that feed and drain these small capillaries begin to have abnormal perfusion and subsequently, structural changes.
keep_reasoning: This fact explains a hypothesized mechanism for progression of microvascular disease in the retina.

fact: Disruptions in blood flow at different levels of the retinal vascular system can have different time courses, with large vessel occlusions causing rapid effects and small capillary disruptions causing slow but severe tissue damage.
source_span: Disruptions at different hierarchies in the retinal vascular system can also have a large temporal bandwidth. These include a translation and replication system for tobamovirus RNA in evacuolated plant cell extract (BYL) [39] and a method to prepare and purify active tobamovirus RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) [27].
keep_reasoning: This explains the experimental approach enabling detailed study of viral replication mechanisms.

fact: Purified ToMV RNA-dependent RNA polymerase preparations contain viral replication proteins, TOM1, TOM2A, HSP70, eEF1A, and an unidentified 20-kDa protein.
source_span: Our previous study showed that the purified ToMV RdRp preparation contained viral replication proteins, TOM1, TOM2A, HSP70, eEF1A, and an unidentified protein of approximately 20 kDa [27].
keep_reasoning: This fact sets the stage for identifying a novel host factor involved in viral replication.

fact: The unidentified 20-kDa protein co-purified with ToMV replication proteins was identified as NtARL8, a small GTP-binding protein.
source_span: We analyzed the 20-kDa protein using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) and found that it was a small GTP-binding protein, NtARL8.
keep_reasoning: Identifying NtARL8 as a host factor is a key novel finding relevant for understanding tobamovirus replication.

fact: NtARL8 co-purifies with ToMV replication proteins from membrane fractions but not from soluble cytoplasmic fractions.

keep_reasoning: This indicates that NtARL8 associates with membrane-bound viral replication complexes, important for understanding its role.

fact: Four ARL8-related genes were identified in Nicotiana tabacum, and proteins from at least three of these genes co-purify with ToMV replication proteins.
source_span: By the degenerate PCR and RACE methods, we identified four ARL8-related genes from N. tabacum cv. Samsun and found by re-analyzing the LC-MS/MS data that the proteins from at least three of these genes, NtARL8a, NtARL8b, and NtARL8c, were co-purified with ToMV 180K-FS.
keep_reasoning: This shows the genetic basis for NtARL8 proteins involved in viral replication.

fact: ARL8 proteins belong to the ARF family of small GTP-binding proteins that have an N-terminal amphipathic helix enabling tight membrane binding.
source_span: ARL8 belongs to the ARF family of small GTP-binding proteins that include ARF and SAR proteins. ARF family proteins have an N-terminal amphipathic helix that participates in tight binding of the protein to membranes.
keep_reasoning: This provides molecular background on ARL8, helping explain its membrane association relevant to viral replication.

fact: ARL8 family genes are conserved in plants and animals but are absent in yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

fact: In animals, ARL8 proteins mainly localize to lysosomes and mediate transport of endocytosed macromolecules by facilitating late endosome-lysosome fusion.
source_span: Human, Drosophila melanogaster, and Caenorhabditis elegans ARL8 proteins mainly localize to lysosomes and C. elegans ARL8 mediates transport of endocytosed macromolecules to lysosomes by facilitating late endosome-lysosome fusion [43]–[45].
